question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-x(t),\end{aligned}\right.\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: $$ \displaystyle {e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}, $$ where $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. $$*
$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$
$2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $$
\displaystyle x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}
$$ and $$
\displaystyle g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$ So, the matrix of the system is $$
\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)=\underbrace{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+\underbrace{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t-s)\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the following inhomogeneous system of linear differential equations: $$ {x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}x(t)+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} $$ The complementary solution to this system is given by $$ {x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R. $$ Then, the general solution of the system is
$x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+\,\,$
{{field-1}}

$\,\,{t}^{2}+\,\,$
$-1$
{{field-3}}
$\,\,t+\,\,$
{{field-2}}
$-2$
$.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

The forcing term

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix}
$$

of the inhomogeneous system of ODEs is polynomial of degree $2.$ Therefore, we assume that the particular solution is also polynomial of degree $2,$ i.e.

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}{b}_{1} \\ {b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

where ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{c}_{1},{c}_{2}$ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the derivative of ${x}_{p}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{x}_{p}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To find the unknown constants, we substitute ${x}_{p}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}$ into our system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -\frac{4}{3} & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}{t}^{2}+{b}_{1}t+{c}_{1} \\ {a}_{2}{t}^{2}+{b}_{2}t+{c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}}{3}\right) \\ \left(\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}}{3}\right)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-6{t}^{2}+\frac{41}{3}t-8 \\ 3{t}^{2}-\frac{13}{3}t+5\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{1}t+{b}_{1} \\ 0{t}^{2}+2{a}_{2}t+{b}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}\left(\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}\right) \\ \left(\frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}\right){t}^{2}+\left(\frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3}\right)t+\left(\frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3}\right)\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding coefficients of like powers of $t,$ we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{1}-8{a}_{2}-18}{3}=0 \\ \frac{-4{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+9}{3}=0 \\ \frac{5{b}_{1}-8{b}_{2}+41}{3}=2{a}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{b}_{1}+{b}_{2}-13}{3}=2{a}_{2} \\ \frac{5{c}_{1}-8{c}_{2}-24}{3}={b}_{1} \\ \frac{-4{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}+15}{3}={b}_{2}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving the first and second equations, we get

$$
{a}_{1}=2,\,{a}_{2}=-1.
$$

Substituting these into the second and third equations, and solving for ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2},$ we get

$$
{b}_{1}=-1,\,{b}_{2}=3.
$$

Finally, substituting these last two values into the fourth and sixth equations, and solving for ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ we have

$$
{c}_{1}=1,\,{c}_{2}=-2.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{t}^{2}-t+1 \\ -{t}^{2}+3t-2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}t+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be re-written as 

$$
{J}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{5}-y+10) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{5}-y+10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-{y}^{2}+3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-{y}^{2}+3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5{x}^{4} & -1 \\ y & x-2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}5{x}^{4} & -1 \\ y & x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{5}-y+10 \\ xy-{y}^{2}+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}5{x}^{4} & -1 \\ y & x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{5}-y+10 \\ xy-{y}^{2}+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}5(-1)^{4} & -1 \\ 1 & (-1)-2(1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{5}-(1)+10 \\ (-1)(1)-{1}^{2}+3\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $$
\displaystyle ({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{23}{14} \\ -\frac{3}{14}\end{bmatrix}.

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-{y}^{2}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-{y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -2y \\ -2x & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -2y \\ -2x & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{3}-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with $$
\displaystyle {x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},
$$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2} & -2y \\ -2x & 3{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{3}-{y}^{2}+1 \\ {y}^{3}-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}3(-1)^{2} & -2(1) \\ -2(-1) & 3(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{3}-{1}^{2}+1 \\ {1}^{3}-(-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 3-2\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{13}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{10}{13} \\ \frac{11}{13}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.769 \\ 0.846\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}

rounded to three decimal places.

The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-6xy-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4x{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-6xy-x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6x-6y-1 \\ 8xy-6x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{y}^{2}+6x-6y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-6x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{y}^{2}+6x-6y-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-6x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8y-6 \\ 8y-6 & 8x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}6 & 8y-6 \\ 8y-6 & 8x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}4{y}^{2}+6x-6y-1 \\ 8xy-6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1$ and $2.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,$
$-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$$-2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t}$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}r(t) &={e}^{t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}).
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\left(\frac{1}{t}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t})\right)t \\  & =-({e}^{2t}-{e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}-{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} & -2{e}^{t}+2{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{t}-{e}^{2t} & 2{e}^{t}-{e}^{2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} &={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′} &={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′} &={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-(t-1){y}^{′}+5\sqrt{t}\,y+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=-{t}^{2}{x}_{3}-(t-1){x}_{2}+5\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side.

$$

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $$
\displaystyle {y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}{0}^{2}+{1}^{2} \\ 0\cdot 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},
$$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues

question.:question/problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $1\pm 2\text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}={e}^{t}\,\,$
$\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)${{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)${{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=(1+2\text{i})t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=(1-2\text{i})t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((1+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(1+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(1+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ ({\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{t}\left(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Matrix

question.:question/problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda$ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
${2}^{({J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2))}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}$0$
$0${{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$0$$0${{field-5}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=\begin{bmatrix}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{bmatrix}.
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{({J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2))} & ={2}^{\left(\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{1}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(2)\end{bmatrix}\right)} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{({J}_{1}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{({J}_{2}(2))}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={2}^{({J}_{1}(1))}\,⊕\,{2}^{({J}_{2}(2))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(1),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ Since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(1)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{(1)}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={2}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{2}^{2} & {2}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & {2}^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{({J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(2))} & ={2}^{({J}_{1}(1))}\,⊕\,{2}^{({J}_{2}(2))} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 4\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Applying the Chain Rule to Calculate Gradients

question.:question/problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2\times 3}\to R$ defined by $L(A)=(2Ax-3b)^{T}(2Ax-3b),$ where $$ x=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}. $$ What is ${∇}_{A}L$ at $$ \displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}? $$
${∇}_{A}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
$-160${{field-4}}$-64$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The gradient of $L$ with respect to $A$ is a matrix of the same shape as $A$, with $(i,j)$th entry given by

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}},
$$

the partial derivative of $L$ with respect to the $(i,j)$th entry of $A.$

We can compute $\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}$ by applying the chain rule.

Let $y=2Ax-3b\in {R}^{2}.$ Then, $L(A)={y}^{T}y$ and

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}}={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}
$$

Now, since 

$$
{∇}_{y}L={∇}_{y}({y}^{T}y)=2y,
$$

we have that

$$
\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}=2{y}_{k}.
$$

Writing out $y=2Ax-3b$ in component-wise notation as 

$$
{y}_{i}=2{\sum }_{j=1}^{3}{a}_{ij}{x}_{j}-3{b}_{i},
$$

we have 

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=2{x}_{j}$ if $i=k$, and

- $\frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}}=0$ if $i\ne k.$

This means that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂L}{∂{a}_{ij}} & ={\sum }_{k=1}^{2}\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{k}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{k}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =\frac{∂L}{∂{y}_{i}}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot \frac{∂{y}_{i}}{∂{a}_{ij}} \\  & =2{y}_{i}\cdot 2{x}_{j} \\  & =4{y}_{i}{x}_{j}\end{aligned}
$$

The $(i,j)$th entry of ${∇}_{A}L$ is $4$ times the $i$th entry of $y$ multiplied by the $j$th entry of $x$, so

$$
{∇}_{A}L=4y\cdot {x}^{T}.
$$

Finally, evaluating ${∇}_{A}L$ at $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{A}L & =4y\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4(2Ax-3b)\cdot {x}^{T} \\  & =4\left(2\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4\left(\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ 18\end{bmatrix}\right)\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-48 \\ -32\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-240 & 0 & -96 \\ -160 & 0 & -64\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$
